name: Phoenix Mars Lander

location.name: Green Valley, Vastitas Borealis (northern arctic plains)

headline: It tasted water ice in the Martian arctic, then fell silent as winter closed in
story: At 23:38 UT on 25 May 2008, Phoenix touched down on a flat valley floor in the far north of Mars. It was the first successful landing in a polar region of the planet. The ground was cracked into polygons, the pattern of frozen soil, and the team expected ice to lie just beneath the surface, within reach of the lander's robotic arm.

On 15 June the arm widened a trench nicknamed Dodo-Goldilocks, leaving dice-sized chunks of bright material at the bottom. Within four days they had vanished, turned straight to vapor. "It must be ice," said principal investigator Peter Smith. On 31 July, an oven aboard the lander heated a scoop of soil and settled it. "We have water," said William Boynton.

Its weather station, Canada's contribution to the mission, detected snow falling from clouds about 4 kilometres above the lander. Phoenix also found perchlorate salt in the soil. Built for three months, it worked for five, until the arctic autumn starved its solar panels. Its last signal arrived on 2 November 2008. In 2010, HiRISE saw that one panel no longer cast a shadow, probably crushed by winter frost. The lander still stands on the plain, coated in dust.

facts.label: A first
facts.value: First successful landing in a polar region of Mars

facts.label: Working life
facts.value: Planned for at least 90 Martian days; worked for more than five months

facts.label: Last signal
facts.value: 2 November 2008, relayed by NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter

images.caption: 15 June 2008: bright water ice exposed in the trench nicknamed Dodo-Goldilocks. The small lumps in its lower left corner vaporized over the next four days.

Seen from orbit by HiRISE: the lander, its heat shield, and its backshell and parachute in July 2008, and again in May 2010. After one winter, all were dusted over, and the lander's western solar panel cast no shadow.
